## Scope

- `CorrSurvGSD` provides a theoretical evaluation of group sequential designs with sequential testing of progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS).
- The Shiny application collects design assumptions and displays the resulting design summary, analysis schedule, decision boundaries, marginal power, and hierarchical joint power.
- This vignette explains the statistical chain behind those results: design inputs determine the survival model, the survival model determines calendar cutoffs and expected event information, and that information determines correlation, boundaries, and power.
- The calculations are closed form at the level of per-subject moments and use numerical root-finding for calendar cutoffs and multivariate-normal integration for crossing probabilities.

## Inputs and notation

- Let `n_T` and `n_C` denote the treatment and control sample sizes, `n=n_T+n_C` the total sample size, and `r=n_T/n_C` the allocation ratio.
- Let \(d_\ell^{PFS}\) be the target number of PFS events at analysis look \(\ell\), for \(\ell=1,\ldots,L\). The targets are strictly increasing and define the number of analysis looks.
- The application accepts either treatment-to-control hazard ratios \((HR_{PFS},HR_{OS})\) or treatment-group median survival times. The control-group median PFS and OS are always supplied.
- Accrual may be constant or piecewise constant. For segment \(i\), let \((t_{i-1},t_i]\) be its calendar interval, \(R_i=t_i-t_{i-1}\) its duration, and \(v_i\) its accrual rate.
- The survival-time unit and the calendar-time unit are shared across the median survival inputs, accrual schedule, and derived analysis cutoffs.
- Each endpoint has an efficacy-look schedule and may have futility looks before the final look. The efficacy boundary may use the O'Brien-Fleming (OF), Pocock, or Hwang-Shih-DeCani (HSD) alpha-spending family. HSD additionally uses an endpoint-specific gamma parameter.
- The hierarchy selects either PFS followed by OS or OS followed by PFS. Optional simulation settings control whether empirical Monte Carlo summaries are calculated in addition to the theoretical results.

For piecewise accrual, the enrollment time \(U\) has density \(v_i/n\) on segment \(i\). The total accrual duration and segment probabilities are represented by

```{=tex}
\begin{equation*}
R=\sum_i R_i, \qquad
\mathbb{P}(U\in(t_{i-1},t_i])=\frac{v_iR_i}{n},
\qquad
\sum_i\frac{v_iR_i}{n}=1.
\end{equation*}
```

- This normalization connects the rates entered in Shiny with the enrollment distribution used by every expectation below.
- The notation \(A_\ell\) denotes the calendar cutoff associated with look \(\ell\), while \(d_\ell^{OS}\) denotes the expected OS event count at that same cutoff.

## Fleischer model and analysis timing

For treatment or control arm \(g\), the Fleischer model uses independent exponential latent progression and death times.

```{=tex}
\begin{equation*}
E_{1g}\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda_{1,g}),\qquad
E_{2g}\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda_{2,g}),\qquad
E_{1g}\perp E_{2g}.
\end{equation*}
```

- \(E_{1g}\) is the latent progression time and \(E_{2g}\) is the latent death time.
- Independence is imposed within an arm, while PFS and OS remain statistically related because PFS includes the same latent death process that defines OS.

The observed endpoint times and their hazards are

```{=tex}
\begin{equation*}
T_g^{PFS}=\min(E_{1g},E_{2g}),\qquad
T_g^{OS}=E_{2g},\qquad
\Lambda_g=\lambda_{1,g}+\lambda_{2,g}.
\end{equation*}
```

- \(\Lambda_g\) is the PFS hazard, and \(\lambda_{2,g}\) is the OS hazard.
- For the control arm, the supplied medians imply the latent hazards through

```{=tex}
\begin{equation*}
\Lambda_C=\frac{\log(2)}{\operatorname{median}_{PFS,C}},
\qquad
\lambda_{2,C}=\frac{\log(2)}{\operatorname{median}_{OS,C}},
\qquad
\lambda_{1,C}=\Lambda_C-\lambda_{2,C}.
\end{equation*}
```

- The treatment arm can be parameterized directly by medians, or by hazard ratios using

```{=tex}
\begin{equation*}
\Lambda_T=HR_{PFS}\Lambda_C,\qquad
\lambda_{2,T}=HR_{OS}\lambda_{2,C},\qquad
\lambda_{1,T}=\Lambda_T-\lambda_{2,T}.
\end{equation*}
```

- The validator requires the resulting latent hazards to be positive and rejects incomplete or conflicting treatment-effect specifications.

For a subject enrolled at time \(U\), follow-up at calendar cutoff \(A\) and the associated observed variables are

```{=tex}
\begin{equation*}
a(A,U)=(A-U)_+,\qquad
\delta^k(A)=\mathbf{1}\{T^k\le a(A,U)\},\qquad
\widetilde T^k(A)=\min\{T^k,a(A,U)\}.
\end{equation*}
```

- \(a(A,U)\) is the available follow-up, so subjects enrolled after \(A\) contribute no follow-up.
- \(\delta^k(A)\) records whether endpoint \(k\) has been observed by the cutoff, and \(\widetilde T^k(A)\) is the administratively truncated time used in the moment calculations.

The PFS target determines each calendar cutoff by matching expected PFS events to the requested event count.

```{=tex}
\begin{equation*}
n_T\,m_{\delta_\ell^{PFS}}^{(T)}(A_\ell)
+n_C\,m_{\delta_\ell^{PFS}}^{(C)}(A_\ell)
=d_\ell^{PFS}.
\end{equation*}
```

- \(m_{\delta_\ell^{PFS}}^{(g)}(A_\ell)\) is the expected PFS event indicator for one subject in arm \(g\) at cutoff \(A_\ell\).
- The application solves this monotone equation for \(A_\ell\) in increasing order, so the result is a calendar analysis schedule rather than an assumed fixed time schedule.

The same calendar cutoffs define the OS information used at each look.

```{=tex}
\begin{equation*}
d_\ell^{OS}
=n_T\,m_{\delta_\ell^{OS}}^{(T)}(A_\ell)
+n_C\,m_{\delta_\ell^{OS}}^{(C)}(A_\ell).
\end{equation*}
```

- \(d_\ell^{OS}\) is an expected event count derived from the PFS-driven cutoff, not an additional user-specified target.
- This coupling allows PFS and OS analyses to use different efficacy or futility look selections while remaining tied to the same calendar schedule.

## Closed-form moments and joint correlation

For endpoint \(k\), arm \(g\), and look \(\ell\), collect the event indicator and truncated follow-up time into

```{=tex}
\begin{equation*}
X_{g,k,\ell}
=\begin{pmatrix}
\delta^k_\ell\\
\widetilde T^k_\ell
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
m_{g,k,\ell}=\mathbb{E}[X_{g,k,\ell}],
\qquad
\Sigma_{g,k,\ell}
=\operatorname{Cov}(X_{g,k,\ell}).
\end{equation*}
```

- The vector \(m_{g,k,\ell}\) supplies the single-look means required for event counts and log-hazard-ratio variance calculations.
- The covariance matrix \(\Sigma_{g,k,\ell}\) is obtained by evaluating the exponential expectations over the piecewise-uniform enrollment distribution.
- The same analytic integration also supplies cross-look products between PFS and OS. For looks \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\), define

```{=tex}
\begin{equation*}
\Sigma_{g,PFS,OS,\ell_1,\ell_2}
=\operatorname{Cov}\left(
X_{g,PFS,\ell_1},X_{g,OS,\ell_2}
\right).
\end{equation*}
```

- This \(2\times2\) cross-look covariance block captures the dependence created by the shared latent death time and by common enrollment timing.
- Subtracting products of the corresponding means converts each analytically evaluated product expectation into the covariance needed downstream.

For each endpoint and look, the log-hazard-ratio approximation uses the map \(h(x_1,x_2)=\log(x_1)-\log(x_2)\). Its gradient at the arm-specific means is

```{=tex}
\begin{equation*}
\nabla h_{g,k,\ell}
=\begin{pmatrix}
1/m_{\delta^k_\ell}^{(g)}\\
-1/m_{\widetilde T^k_\ell}^{(g)}
\end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation*}
```

- The gradient translates variation in event counts and person-time into variation in the estimated log hazard ratio.
- The Delta method then combines the treatment and control contributions.

The resulting marginal variance at endpoint \(k\), look \(\ell\), is

```{=tex}
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\theta}^k_\ell)
=\sum_{g\in\{T,C\}}
\frac{1}{n_g}
\nabla h_{g,k,\ell}^{\mathsf T}
\Sigma_{g,k,\ell}
\nabla h_{g,k,\ell}.
\end{equation*}
```

- \(\widehat{\theta}^k_\ell\) is the estimated log hazard ratio at that endpoint and look.
- The sample-size factors scale per-subject covariance to the two-arm estimator variance.

The cross-endpoint covariance between PFS look \(\ell_1\) and OS look \(\ell_2\) is

```{=tex}
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat{\theta}^{PFS}_{\ell_1},
\widehat{\theta}^{OS}_{\ell_2})
=\sum_{g\in\{T,C\}}
\frac{1}{n_g}
\nabla h_{g,PFS,\ell_1}^{\mathsf T}
\Sigma_{g,PFS,OS,\ell_1,\ell_2}
\nabla h_{g,OS,\ell_2}.
\end{equation*}
```

- Standardizing this covariance by the two marginal standard deviations produces the PFS/OS correlations.
- Within an endpoint, the canonical group-sequential correlation uses the information represented by expected events.

```{=tex}
\begin{equation*}
\rho^k_{\ell_1,\ell_2}
=\sqrt{
\frac{d^k_{\min(\ell_1,\ell_2)}}
{d^k_{\max(\ell_1,\ell_2)}}}.
\end{equation*}
```

- Combining the within-endpoint correlations with the standardized cross-endpoint covariances gives the joint correlation matrix for the multivariate normal Z vector.
- Its ordering is PFS looks first and OS looks second, with one diagonal entry for each endpoint-look statistic.

## Sequential boundaries and theoretical power

The assumed hazard ratio determines the mean Z-score drift at each endpoint and look.

```{=tex}
\begin{equation*}
\theta^k_\ell
=-\log(HR_k)
\sqrt{\frac{d^k_\ell r}{(1+r)^2}},
\qquad
r=\frac{n_T}{n_C}.
\end{equation*}
```

- A treatment benefit with \(HR_k<1\) gives positive drift in the direction of the one-sided efficacy boundary.
- PFS uses \(d_\ell^{PFS}\), while OS uses the derived \(d_\ell^{OS}\), so their drift vectors can differ even at the same calendar look.

The selected alpha-spending family determines the efficacy boundaries at the configured looks.

- OF, Pocock, and HSD are selectable endpoint-specific spending families.
- The one-sided alpha level controls the total efficacy spending, while HSD gamma controls how spending is distributed across looks.
- Futility boundaries are created only at selected pre-final futility looks and are obtained from the corresponding futility hazard-ratio thresholds.
- The boundary table displayed by Shiny reports both endpoints on Z, hazard-ratio, and one-sided p-value scales.

For information \(d^k_\ell\), define \(s^k_\ell\) as the information scale of the log-hazard-ratio statistic. A finite Z boundary converts as

```{=tex}
\begin{equation*}
s^k_\ell
=\sqrt{\frac{d^k_\ell r}{(1+r)^2}},
\qquad
HR^k_\ell
=\exp\left(-\frac{Z^k_\ell}{s^k_\ell}\right),
\qquad
p^k_\ell=1-\Phi(Z^k_\ell).
\end{equation*}
```

- \(HR^k_\ell\) is the hazard-ratio threshold equivalent to the Z boundary, and \(p^k_\ell\) is its one-sided p-value.
- Unconfigured boundaries remain infinite on the Z scale and are unavailable on the displayed HR and p scales.

For endpoint \(k\), the incremental marginal power at efficacy look \(\ell\) is the probability of first crossing there.

```{=tex}
\begin{equation*}
\pi^k_\ell
=\mathbb{P}\left(
c^k_j\le Z^k_j<a^k_j\ \text{for all }j<\ell,
\quad Z^k_\ell\ge a^k_\ell
\right).
\end{equation*}
```

- \(a^k_j\) is the efficacy boundary and \(c^k_j\) is the futility boundary, with infinite values representing an unconfigured boundary.
- The probability is evaluated under the endpoint-specific mean drift and within-endpoint correlation matrix.
- Summing the mutually exclusive incremental probabilities gives cumulative marginal power through look \(\ell\).

With a fixed testing hierarchy, joint power requires a primary efficacy crossing followed by a secondary efficacy crossing at the same or a later look.

```{=tex}
\begin{equation*}
\operatorname{Power}_{joint}
=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\sum_{j=\ell}^{L}
\mathbb{P}\left(
E^{primary}_\ell\cap E^{secondary}_{j\mid\ell}
\right).
\end{equation*}
```

- \(E^{primary}_\ell\) is the primary endpoint's first efficacy-crossing event at look \(\ell\).
- \(E^{secondary}_{j\mid\ell}\) is the secondary endpoint's first eligible efficacy-crossing event at look \(j\), conditional on the hierarchy opening at look \(\ell\).
- The displayed joint-power matrix records each crossing pair, and its cells sum to the reported hierarchical joint power.
- The full PFS/OS joint correlation matrix and the two drift vectors define the multivariate normal probabilities used for these cells.

## Simulation and reproducibility

- Simulation is optional and is used to compare empirical Monte Carlo summaries with the closed-form results under the same Fleischer assumptions.
- When enabled, the application reports simulated counterparts for marginal and joint power while retaining the theoretical boundary and power calculations.
- The `integration_seed` controls reproducible multivariate-normal integration for the theoretical crossing probabilities.
- The `simulation_seed` controls reproducible empirical summaries, and `n_sim` controls the requested number of Monte Carlo replicates.
- The computational tolerance controls the numerical solution of the calendar-cutoff equations, while display precision affects presentation only.
- The Shiny results can be reviewed as design summary, boundary, and power views, and the displayed result tables can be exported as CSV without changing the underlying calculations.
